title: Animal Farm, George Orwell
subject: litterature
description: In 1945, Orwell tells the story of a farm where the animals drive out the farmer, then watch the pigs take his place. A crystal-clear allegory of the Russian Revolution and of a revolution betrayed.

hero.hook: Thirty thousand words, a few farm animals, and a political lesson the world still has not learned.

blocks.text: Published in **1945**, **Animal Farm** looks like a children's story. Behind that simple surface, **George Orwell** shows how a popular revolution can be stolen by a corrupt elite. In barely **30,000 words**, he builds one of the sharpest political fables ever written, a point-by-point **[[Allegory of the Russian Revolution]]**.

blocks.caption: Pigs in power: the fable that exposes revolutionary corruption

sections.title: A surgical allegory of Soviet history

blocks.text: The book was written during the **[[Second World War]]**, while the USSR was still the ally of the West against Nazi Germany. Criticizing **Stalin** then looked like political treason, so Orwell waited for the war to end before publishing. Every animal stands for a historical figure: **Old Major** echoes **Marx** and **Lenin**, **Napoleon** is modeled on **Stalin**, and **Snowball** recalls **Trotsky**, Stalin's rival, exiled and later murdered.
T.S. Eliot, then an editor at Faber, turned the manuscript down. His objection: clever pigs might offend statesmen.

Napoleon's **dogs** stand for the secret police and for political terror. **Boxer**, the tireless carthorse, embodies a **[[proletariat]]** worked to complete exhaustion. **Squealer**, the pig propagandist, turns every failure into an official victory and rewrites history day by day. Orwell pins down **[[Stalinism]]** with the precision of a pamphlet and the lightness of a fable.

sections.title: The turning point: from utopia to dictatorship

blocks.text: The animals drive out farmer **Jones**, the stand-in for **[[Tsar Nicholas II]]**, overthrown in **1917**. They proclaim **Animalism** and paint the **Seven Commandments** on the barn wall. Equality finally looks possible. Then Napoleon chases Snowball off the farm with dogs trained to attack, and installs terror in his place.

blocks.caption: The farm at the start: a utopia sliding into dictatorship

blocks.text: The windmill becomes a symbol of forced labor: the animals wear themselves out building it while the pigs declare themselves “intellectual workers” and take the resources for themselves. Apples and milk go first to the leaders, in the name of the “brain” that has to be fed. Corruption starts with small privileges, then hardens into a rule. The show trials and the executions echo the Stalinist **great purges** of the 1930s.

sections.title: Rewriting the language, and the final betrayal

blocks.text: Orwell shows that whoever controls the words controls what people believe is real. The pigs edit the Commandments at night, while the animals sleep: “No animal shall sleep in a bed” quietly becomes “no animal shall sleep in a bed with sheets.” The ban on alcohol gains the words “to excess.” Collective memory is erased one word at a time, until nobody remembers the original.
All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others.

This is **[[Newspeak]]** before its time: language no longer communicates, it hides. At the end, the pigs walk on two legs, wear clothes and feast with human farmers. The other animals look from pig to man and from man to pig, and can no longer tell them apart. The **[[Russian Revolution]]** produced exactly what it claimed to be fighting.

The book aims at the Russian Revolution first, but its message goes far beyond Soviet history. Orwell examines obedience, propaganda, and how fragile ideals become once personal ambition takes over. Without a critical education and without collective memory, a people watches its dreams of freedom hijacked by those who seize power in its name.

With more than **30 million** copies sold, the novel reaches readers of every age and every culture. As a child you read a story about animals; as an adult you read a treatise on politics. The lesson stays simple and current: when words lose their meaning, physical freedom soon follows. Orwell is already preparing here the themes he would push to the extreme in **1984** four years later.
**Animal Farm** shows that a betrayed revolution runs on manipulated language and confiscated memory. Orwell proves that a short fable can say more than a thousand-page speech.
